Drought Aid

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
They are called the ‘fodder boys.’ A group of youngsters from the Cape flats giving hope to farmers who are facing the worst drought in 200 years and are unable to feed their animals.

Unique Selling Point:
Farmers are on their knees praying for rain. Drought has taken its toll in large parts of the country. Sutherland has seen the worst: farmers have sold their prize animals for as little as R30 to avoid starvation.

Hope came in the form of the fodder boys: A group of young men rescued from Hannover on the Cape Flats by an NGO who are now delivering feed to desperate farmers in drought crisis. In Sutherland alone sheep stock have dropped from 400 000 to 104 000. Some farmers have sold up their last belongings and moved to start a new life, but for most of them there is no alternative. Farming is in their blood and survive they will. The fodder boys have changed their lives and made it bearable as they receive feed to keep their animals alive until the rain comes back again.


Summary:
Imtiaz Sooliman is the founder Gift of the Givers, a nonprofit organisation that move into areas where disaster has struck and people have lost everything. Instead of despair, they bring relief. From victims of fire to areas where drought has claimed its toll, they work tirelessly to help those in need.

In January this year Sooliman looked at the youngsters in Hannover who live in fear of gangsters and drug lords and tasked Ali Sablay from the organization to select a group of youngsters from Hanover Park to join the organisation as volunteers. The Western Cape has been called the murder capital of South Africa. Ten of the 30 police stations with the highest incidence of murder are found in this province and 808 gang related murders alone last year. For the community of Hannover there is little hope of leading a peaceful life and the prospect of work. It is against this landscape that Sablay took the 10 youngsters under his wing. None of them had any prospect of work but already the burden of responsibility were weighing heavily on their shoulders; parents and younger siblings were looking at them to put bread on the table. Set against this backdrop the fodder boys were formed and started working for Gift of the Givers.

Further information:
Since January this year the fodder boys have made a difference to many people’s lives: from delivering blankets and food to victims of fire who have nothing left, to seeing the hope of farmers when they deliver feed for their cattle and sheep, the goodwill they spread in turn has given them hope that life is worth fighting for.

Then in the first week of October, hours after delivering feed to the farmers in the Eastern Cape one of them, 20 year old Ameerudeen Noordien was caught in a gangster crossfire. Bystanders were shouting “run for your life” but he was deaf in one ear and could not hear. Hours later he died in his sister’s arms. He was the breadwinner for his elderly parents and two younger siblings. Keanu Pieterson, a close friend of Ameerudeen was heartbroken. He has been counselled to get over the trauma of his best friend’s senseless death. But through this traumatic event, the fodder boys have only grown stronger in spirit and will to make a difference out there by giving to those in need.

We will hear about the circumstances from 19 year old Keanu Baartman who have to take care of his mother and two siblings at school. For him it has been hard to carry on without Ameerudien. “I will never forget him. He was my best friend. But Gift of the Givers have been good to me and working with the farmers.”

Another youngster in the Fodder boys group is Riaan Mathews. He is the breadwinner and takes care of his parents and says that without this job he would have still been on the streets of Hannover. “There is no work. This has given me hope.”

Farmers have grown to look forward to the arrival of the fodder boys and some have built a closer connection with these youngsters who come from a world that neither has experienced
It is hours before the arrival of the trucks from Gift of the Giverers. Already a hand full of farmers are lining up with their bakkies and trailers at a mutual collection point here on a farm in Sutherland where the feed will be dropped off. With smiles they greet the youngsters who they have come to know and handshakes follow. Eager to please, the fodder boys get to work and offload the bales of hay onto the trailers.

The story:
Today is one of many days where the fodder boys show their metal. Hester Obermeyer is the coordinator of the drought project for the Cape and have seen the difference it made to the farmer’s morale since the fodder boys have been coming to town. “The impact that the fodder boys have had on this community alone has been an eye opener. It is like the guys have equalised the playing field where mutual respect for one another has been shown,” she says. “We are very sad to hear about Ameerudeen. He was one of my favourites.”

One of the farmers from the area, Jan van Wyk, who have been close to the boys express his sadness about the senseless death of Ameerudeen but in the same breath cannot stop talking about the good work the fodder boys do. A woman standing close by overhear the conversation and express her gratitude for the feed they have delivered. Ilse Demanndi has been heartbroken to see how the drought has destroyed their crop and took the toll on their sheep. “We cannot survive without the feed that we get for our animals. Already we have no more overdraft facility with the bank and their is still no prospect of rain. Over the last 4 years we have lost almost everything. All we have left is hope that we will get through this crisis”, she says.

For the last four years Obermeyer has been organising bales of feed for the Cape from farmers across South Africa who are prepared to sell it at the cost price of R80 per bale. She coordinates the collection and delivery points in the Cape. “The hard part is to select which region is next to take care of. The situation is so dire that can we only say thank you to people like Gift of the Givers who donate their transport vehicles to us at no charge. We get feed from as far as KwaZulu Natal and the Free-state where the goodwill of the farmers who can afford it have been phoning me with their quota for pickup,” she says.

The fodder boys:
19 Year old Keanu Baartman has been taken care of his mother and two siblings at school. For him it has been hard to carry on without Ameerudien. “I will never forget him. He was my best friend. But Gift of the Givers have been good to me and working with the farmers.”

Another youngster in the Fodder boy group is Riaan Mathews. He has to care of his parents and says that this job is all he has. “They found me on the streets in January. This job is all I have”, he says.

Treatment:
The story will be told through the eyes of the fodder boys who give and the farmers who receive. The relationships built through this drought relief intervention and the personal circumstances of how through adversity comes hope.

Press Release:


A Helping Hand
The drought has taken its toll in large parts of the country and farmers in the Karoo are still on their knees praying for rain. Sutherland has seen the worst; farmers have had to sell their prized livestock for as little as R30 to avoid starvation. Now a group of young men rescued from the Cape Flats where communities are held hostage by gangs that rule the streets, are giving hope to these farmers and helping them survive one of the worst droughts of a century.
Producer: Annalise Lubbe
Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli
Watch the trailer


Script:


Script: The Fodder Boys - “Volunteers of the Givers”
Date: 13 November 2018
Duration: 10 minutes

Up audio: Driving shot

Link: We have been driving through the Karoo for the past hour. This is an area that at some stage had close to 400 000 sheep and throughout the entire drive i have not seen a single one.

Up audio - drive through farm gates. Cut to drone shot of dry dam. AJ Burger on the whistle calling his sheep.

V/O AJ Burger has been farming sheep for generations on Fraserburg Road, north of Sutherland, but now his dams have run dry and, to keep his remaining flock alive, he must feed them by hand.

Macfarlane Moleli: Major hoe lank was jy al in die karoo? (Major how long have you been here in the Karoo?)

AJ Burger - Farmer: Mac, ek het hier begin boer in 1977. Dis die ergste droogte wat ons nou beleef. (I started farming here in 1977. This drought is the worst we’ve experienced) Mac ons is desperaat vir hulp. Ons boere kan nie verder nie. (We are desperate for help. The farmers cannot go on) Ons het nie kos vir ons diere nie. (We don’t have feed for our animals).

Macfarlane Moleli: Is daar mense wat maar net hulle goete opgepak het en gelos het? (Are there people who have just packed up and left?)

AJ Burger: Hier is al boere. Hier is jong boere wat nie meer kan aangaan nie wat kinders het en mense wie se uitgawes is groot. (We have young farmers who cannot go on any more; they have children and huge expenses), maar jy kom op n punt dan kom jy nie verder nie (but you get to a point where you can’t continue)

Link: We are 90 km north of Sutherland on a farm in the Karoo where a devastated community endures the worst drought in a century. The famished livestock, parched earth and clouds of dust have the farmers on their knees, praying for rain to fall.

V/O The average age of a farmer in the Karoo is in the sixties. Abraham van Wyk is one of only a few young people who have returned to the family farm in the hope of succeeding in a challenging business.

Macfarlane Moleli: Abraham, how long have you been in this area on the farm?

Abraham van Wyk; Farmer - Einde 2002 is my oupa oorlede toe het ek terug gekom plaas toe en my oupa het voor hy dood is al vir my gese (In 2002 when my grandfather died I returned to the farm and before my grandfather died he said) “my boeta twee goeters waarvan jy seker is in ons wereld, is dood en droogte”.(My son, there are two things in this world you can be certain of, death and drought) Ons is gewoond aan periodieke droogtes maar ons is nie gewoond aan die tipe droogte wat ons nou het nie. (We are used to periodic drought but we are not use to this type of drought that we are experiencing now). Voer gee is een ding maar dis heeldag, al dag, elke dag. (feeding is one thing, but this is all day, every day)

Up audio:...een duisend en 8

V/O Dr Gideon Groenewald is a geologist with 40 years’ experience in finding water in arid regions. He’s been working in the Sutherland area for the last few months drilling boreholes up to 84 metres deep in search of water bearing rock or aquifers.

Dr Gideon Groenewald: Geologist: Mense dink die Karoo is droog (People think the Karoo is dry), maar die Karoo, is saam met Suid Afrika en saam met Australia is ons in n 220jare dorre sieklus (but the Karoo, as in South Africa and Australia are in a 220 year dry cycle) Ons is aan die einde van n sieklus dit beteken ons gaan ongeveer 10 droe jare met abnormale lae reenval beleef. (We are at the end of the cycle which means we are going to experience ten dry years of abnormal low rainfall).

Macfarlane Moleli: So oom Gideon how do you know where to get water with this machine?

Dr Gideon Groenewald: Hierdie masjien is n magnetometer, hy meet die magneet veld van die aarde (This machine is a magnetometer; it measures the magnetic field of the earth). N kraak in die grond het n ander magneet veld as die totale veld van die aarde. (A fracture in the underlying geology has a different magnetic field compared to its surroundings) Dan meet ek elke meter n lesing (I take a measurement every meter) en dit se vir my waar daar n kraak is en waar daar n kraak is is daar n kans dat ek kan water kry. (and that tells me where there is a fracture, and where there is a fracture, there is the possibility of water).

Macfarlane Moleli: Have you found any water?

Dr Gideon Groenewald: Ons het al 144 punt geboor waarvan 119 susksesvolle boorgate is (We have drilled 144 points of which 119 boreholes have been successful).

Macfarlane Moleli: How much will it help the farmers though if this happens?

Dr Gideon Groenewald: As ons die boere nie help nie gaan ons 104 duisend ooie moet slag voordat hulle van die dors doodgaan. (If we don’t help the farmers we will have to slaughter 104 000 ewes before they die of thirst).

Macfarlane Moleli: Have you lost any animals? How has it affected you personally?

Abraham van Wyk: Mac, ek het geglo ek kan enige dier red. Met die droogte het dit my geleer daar is baie wat ek nie kan red nie. (Mac I believed I could save any animal. This drought has taught me there are many I cannot save).

V/O As the farmers battle to hold on to their livelihoods and livestock, battles of a different kind are being waged 500km away in Hanover Park on the outskirts of Cape Town: battles over drugs, battles over territory. With one of the highest murder rates in the Western Cape, it’s an exceptionally bleak place to live where the only thing you can be sure of is that at the end of most weeks, more people will have been lost to the relentless crime.

Link: Hanover Park is a township in the Cape Flats where the community here is held hostage by drugs and gangsterism and no-one can escape the cycle of violence: gangs, drugs, violence, rob families and remove hope from the youth.

Riaan Matthews - Gift of the Givers volunteer: When I am at home walking on the streets anything bad can happen any time. Like I am here i must always look behind here I must look when are they coming here, when are they going to shoot so I must always be awake and look out for this gangsters.

V/O It’s an all too familiar picture in Hanover Park where people like Riaan Matthews live in fear and face unemployment.

Up natural sound

V/O In January though, things changed for him when Gift of the Givers, a non-profit organisation, chose 10 young people from Hanover Park to work as volunteers. The drought in Sutherland meant farmers needed feed for their livestock. The Hanover Park youngsters were now employed.

Riaan Matthews: Before I joined Gift of the Givers I was just sitting at home. Everyday I had nothing to do, boring life. Living at home, I had no income.

V/O The group of 10 youngsters are all from the same area. Keanu Baartman, lives around the corner from Mathews.

Macfarlane Moleli: What did you do before you joined Gift of the Givers?

Keanu Baartman - Gift of the Givers volunteer: I did not work. I was just laying at home the whole day. Struggling here. Life is hard here.

Macfarlane Moleli: Has working with Gift of the Givers at least helped? Has it changed things at home?

Keanu Baartman: Yeh it changed a lot of things. I it is better. I can move on now.

V/O It’s Friday morning, 2 kilometres outside Sutherland. A convoy of trucks is on its way to deliver feed to the farmers. Leading the convoy are the volunteers.

Link: Well it was a quiet morning here in the Karoo and everything changed as soon as these trucks arrived. Everyone had been waiting for them in anticipation and it is quite nice to see that two worlds are meeting; these guys from Hanover Park coming here to bring hope to the farmers but the farmers also bringing hope to these guys to show that there is life outside of Hanover Park.

V/O Ali Sablay has been mentoring the group of young men from Hanover Park since they started working as volunteers for Gift of the Givers helping farming communities across the western, southern and eastern Cape.

Ali Sablay: Project leader Gift of the Givers: You must remember some of these youths they were just sitting around on the streets; there where their only role models are gangsters and drug dealers. So this has taught them skills, show them how to interact with different communities and of course the most important thing, be able to provide meals and comfort for their families.

V/O Hester Obermeyer works closely with Gift of the Givers. She is in charge of the drought intervention project in Sutherland coordinating the collection and transport of the animal feed donated by farmers from across the country.

Macfarlane Moleli: So where does all your feed come from. Who are the people that have been helping you?

Hester Obermeyer: Sutherland drought coordinator: Our fodder comes from all over the country actually. We have got people from KwaZulu-Natal, Lichtenburg, Schweizer-reneke, Bothaville, Paul Roux. Because the drought in the Karoo is so wide-spread there is no fodder anywhere near us so everything has to be brought in like 1000 km away.

Macfarlane Moleli: How many people is it helping and how bad is the situation in Sutherland?

Hester Obermeyer: In Sutherland we have a 141 farmers on the list. When the drought started we were on 400 000 sheep in this district, we are down to 104 000. We cannot survive without donations any more. It is our lifeline.

V/O For the farmers of Sutherland driving to the feed delivering point has become routine.

Abraham van Wyk: Hierdie voer wat mens ontvang wat van die skenkers af kom is n klein pleistertjie op die ergste seer (The feed we receive from the donors is a small plaster on the worst sore) maar daai pleisterjie is omdat jy sien die mooi in mense se harte om te sien dat die Here nog in mense se hart werk. (but that plaster is because you see the kindness in the hearts of people... that God is still working in their hearts.)

Up audio - greetings and prayer: “Thank you for every mealie pip…”

V/O When the young men are back in Hanover Park, life returns to normal – it is still fragile and dangerous, only now they have been somewhere, they have seen a different sort of hardship in a drought-stricken land and they have helped. And now working for Gift of the Givers they may take heart in the opportunity to become breadwinners for their families.

Macfarlane Moleli: And what is it like interacting with the farmers or the people you go and help?

Riaan Mathews: For me it is something nice because you are helping people that needs the stuff so for me it is almost like a blessing I am receiving. And in there faces you can see they are really happy when you come there by them.

Macfarlane Moleli: What is it like leaving Hanover and then going to meet the farmers and interacting?

Keanu Baartman: It is a wonderful experience. We see stuff we never see. The animals and so. It is great man because we are just almost in a corner here in Hanover park so it is great exploring.

Riaan Mathews: There wasn't an income for me. I got married so now I can help my wife; I can help my baby with whatever he wants.

Mac hugs.

V/O Sadly, one of the volunteers of the Givers, Ameerodien Noordien, was killed in October this year when he was caught in gang crossfire.

Macfarlane Moleli: Tell me about the day Ameerodien got shot. Were you with him?

Keanu Baartman; Yeh I was with him. In fact it was here opposite by the shop. He just went into the shop to buy something. He didn't get a chance to buy. I just heard a lot of shots so when I look it was him and he was dead on the spot.

Ali Sablay: He was caught in a gang crossfire where unfortunately he was deaf in the one ear so when people shouted run, they started to shoot, the time he turned around it was too late. He already had 4 bullets pumped into him and he died immediately on the scene.

V/O Prompted by Noordien’s sad fate, the farmers have created a fund to give something back to a community that has touched their lives.

AJ Burger: Toe het ons daai tragiese ongeluk gehad van die fodder boys wat die voer vir ons kom aflaai wat toe nou doodgeskiet is in Hanover Park (we had the tragic death of one of the fodder boys who delivered the feed) en ons boere het toe besluit (and we as farmers decided) Dit is eintlik erg om te dink dat mense wat jou help word doodgeskiet en ons het n fonds geskiet vir sy familie om hulle te help. (It is actually bad to think that people who help you are getting killed. We created a fund for the family to help them) So ek wil net se onder elke gebleikte hemp is nog n warm hart vir suid afrika se gemeenskap. (So I just want to say: there is a warm heart beating underneath every worn shirt for the community of South Africa).
___________________________________________________________________________

We’ve brought feed for you.”) En die droogte het daarin n rol gespeel om verskillende mense ook bymekaar te bring. (And the drought has played a role in this to bring different people together.) Hulle bring hoop; hulle bring n lekker atmosfeer wanneer die voer afgelaai word. Dis lekker om met die manne te werk. (They bring hope and a lovely atmosphere when the feed is offloaded. It is nice to work with them.)

Author Last Updated 25 November 2018 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 03 December 2018 Press Release: A Helping Hand The drought has taken its toll in large parts of the country and farmers in the Karoo are still on their knees praying for rain. Sutherland has seen the worst; farmers have had to sell their prized livestock for as little as R30 to avoid starvation. Now a group of young men rescued from the Cape Flats where communities are held hostage by gangs that rule the streets, are giving hope to these farmers and helping them survive one of the worst droughts of a century. Producer: Annalise Lubbe Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli Watch the trailer Script: Script: The Fodder Boys - “Volunteers of the Givers” Date: 13 November 2018 Duration: 10 minutes Up audio: Driving shot Link: We have been driving through the Karoo for the past hour. This is an area that at some stage had close to 400 000 sheep and throughout the entire drive i have not seen a single one. Up audio - drive through farm gates. Cut to drone shot of dry dam. AJ Burger on the whistle calling his sheep. V/O AJ Burger has been farming sheep for generations on Fraserburg Road, north of Sutherland, but now his dams have run dry and, to keep his remaining flock alive, he must feed them by hand. Macfarlane Moleli: Major hoe lank was jy al in die karoo? (Major how long have you been here in the Karoo?) AJ Burger - Farmer: Mac, ek het hier begin boer in 1977. Dis die ergste droogte wat ons nou beleef. (I started farming here in 1977. This drought is the worst we’ve experienced) Mac ons is desperaat vir hulp. Ons boere kan nie verder nie. (We are desperate for help. The farmers cannot go on) Ons het nie kos vir ons diere nie. (We don’t have feed for our animals). Macfarlane Moleli: Is daar mense wat maar net hulle goete opgepak het en gelos het? (Are there people who have just packed up and left?) AJ Burger: Hier is al boere. Hier is jong boere wat nie meer kan aangaan nie wat kinders het en mense wie se uitgawes is groot. (We have young farmers who cannot go on any more; they have children and huge expenses), maar jy kom op n punt dan kom jy nie verder nie (but you get to a point where you can’t continue) Link: We are 90 km north of Sutherland on a farm in the Karoo where a devastated community endures the worst drought in a century. The famished livestock, parched earth and clouds of dust have the farmers on their knees, praying for rain to fall. V/O The average age of a farmer in the Karoo is in the sixties. Abraham van Wyk is one of only a few young people who have returned to the family farm in the hope of succeeding in a challenging business. Macfarlane Moleli: Abraham, how long have you been in this area on the farm? Abraham van Wyk; Farmer - Einde 2002 is my oupa oorlede toe het ek terug gekom plaas toe en my oupa het voor hy dood is al vir my gese (In 2002 when my grandfather died I returned to the farm and before my grandfather died he said) “my boeta twee goeters waarvan jy seker is in ons wereld, is dood en droogte”.(My son, there are two things in this world you can be certain of, death and drought) Ons is gewoond aan periodieke droogtes maar ons is nie gewoond aan die tipe droogte wat ons nou het nie. (We are used to periodic drought but we are not use to this type of drought that we are experiencing now). Voer gee is een ding maar dis heeldag, al dag, elke dag. (feeding is one thing, but this is all day, every day) Up audio:...een duisend en 8 V/O Dr Gideon Groenewald is a geologist with 40 years’ experience in finding water in arid regions. He’s been working in the Sutherland area for the last few months drilling boreholes up to 84 metres deep in search of water bearing rock or aquifers. Dr Gideon Groenewald: Geologist: Mense dink die Karoo is droog (People think the Karoo is dry), maar die Karoo, is saam met Suid Afrika en saam met Australia is ons in n 220jare dorre sieklus (but the Karoo, as in South Africa and Australia are in a 220 year dry cycle) Ons is aan die einde van n sieklus dit beteken ons gaan ongeveer 10 droe jare met abnormale lae reenval beleef. (We are at the end of the cycle which means we are going to experience ten dry years of abnormal low rainfall). Macfarlane Moleli: So oom Gideon how do you know where to get water with this machine? Dr Gideon Groenewald: Hierdie masjien is n magnetometer, hy meet die magneet veld van die aarde (This machine is a magnetometer; it measures the magnetic field of the earth). N kraak in die grond het n ander magneet veld as die totale veld van die aarde. (A fracture in the underlying geology has a different magnetic field compared to its surroundings) Dan meet ek elke meter n lesing (I take a measurement every meter) en dit se vir my waar daar n kraak is en waar daar n kraak is is daar n kans dat ek kan water kry. (and that tells me where there is a fracture, and where there is a fracture, there is the possibility of water). Macfarlane Moleli: Have you found any water? Dr Gideon Groenewald: Ons het al 144 punt geboor waarvan 119 susksesvolle boorgate is (We have drilled 144 points of which 119 boreholes have been successful). Macfarlane Moleli: How much will it help the farmers though if this happens? Dr Gideon Groenewald: As ons die boere nie help nie gaan ons 104 duisend ooie moet slag voordat hulle van die dors doodgaan. (If we don’t help the farmers we will have to slaughter 104 000 ewes before they die of thirst). Macfarlane Moleli: Have you lost any animals? How has it affected you personally? Abraham van Wyk: Mac, ek het geglo ek kan enige dier red. Met die droogte het dit my geleer daar is baie wat ek nie kan red nie. (Mac I believed I could save any animal. This drought has taught me there are many I cannot save). V/O As the farmers battle to hold on to their livelihoods and livestock, battles of a different kind are being waged 500km away in Hanover Park on the outskirts of Cape Town: battles over drugs, battles over territory. With one of the highest murder rates in the Western Cape, it’s an exceptionally bleak place to live where the only thing you can be sure of is that at the end of most weeks, more people will have been lost to the relentless crime. Link: Hanover Park is a township in the Cape Flats where the community here is held hostage by drugs and gangsterism and no-one can escape the cycle of violence: gangs, drugs, violence, rob families and remove hope from the youth. Riaan Matthews - Gift of the Givers volunteer: When I am at home walking on the streets anything bad can happen any time. Like I am here i must always look behind here I must look when are they coming here, when are they going to shoot so I must always be awake and look out for this gangsters. V/O It’s an all too familiar picture in Hanover Park where people like Riaan Matthews live in fear and face unemployment. Up natural sound V/O In January though, things changed for him when Gift of the Givers, a non-profit organisation, chose 10 young people from Hanover Park to work as volunteers. The drought in Sutherland meant farmers needed feed for their livestock. The Hanover Park youngsters were now employed. Riaan Matthews: Before I joined Gift of the Givers I was just sitting at home. Everyday I had nothing to do, boring life. Living at home, I had no income. V/O The group of 10 youngsters are all from the same area. Keanu Baartman, lives around the corner from Mathews. Macfarlane Moleli: What did you do before you joined Gift of the Givers? Keanu Baartman - Gift of the Givers volunteer: I did not work. I was just laying at home the whole day. Struggling here. Life is hard here. Macfarlane Moleli: Has working with Gift of the Givers at least helped? Has it changed things at home? Keanu Baartman: Yeh it changed a lot of things. I it is better. I can move on now. V/O It’s Friday morning, 2 kilometres outside Sutherland. A convoy of trucks is on its way to deliver feed to the farmers. Leading the convoy are the volunteers. Link: Well it was a quiet morning here in the Karoo and everything changed as soon as these trucks arrived. Everyone had been waiting for them in anticipation and it is quite nice to see that two worlds are meeting; these guys from Hanover Park coming here to bring hope to the farmers but the farmers also bringing hope to these guys to show that there is life outside of Hanover Park. V/O Ali Sablay has been mentoring the group of young men from Hanover Park since they started working as volunteers for Gift of the Givers helping farming communities across the western, southern and eastern Cape. Ali Sablay: Project leader Gift of the Givers: You must remember some of these youths they were just sitting around on the streets; there where their only role models are gangsters and drug dealers. So this has taught them skills, show them how to interact with different communities and of course the most important thing, be able to provide meals and comfort for their families. V/O Hester Obermeyer works closely with Gift of the Givers. She is in charge of the drought intervention project in Sutherland coordinating the collection and transport of the animal feed donated by farmers from across the country. Macfarlane Moleli: So where does all your feed come from. Who are the people that have been helping you? Hester Obermeyer: Sutherland drought coordinator: Our fodder comes from all over the country actually. We have got people from KwaZulu-Natal, Lichtenburg, Schweizer-reneke, Bothaville, Paul Roux. Because the drought in the Karoo is so wide-spread there is no fodder anywhere near us so everything has to be brought in like 1000 km away. Macfarlane Moleli: How many people is it helping and how bad is the situation in Sutherland? Hester Obermeyer: In Sutherland we have a 141 farmers on the list. When the drought started we were on 400 000 sheep in this district, we are down to 104 000. We cannot survive without donations any more. It is our lifeline. V/O For the farmers of Sutherland driving to the feed delivering point has become routine. Abraham van Wyk: Hierdie voer wat mens ontvang wat van die skenkers af kom is n klein pleistertjie op die ergste seer (The feed we receive from the donors is a small plaster on the worst sore) maar daai pleisterjie is omdat jy sien die mooi in mense se harte om te sien dat die Here nog in mense se hart werk. (but that plaster is because you see the kindness in the hearts of people... that God is still working in their hearts.) Up audio - greetings and prayer: “Thank you for every mealie pip…” V/O When the young men are back in Hanover Park, life returns to normal – it is still fragile and dangerous, only now they have been somewhere, they have seen a different sort of hardship in a drought-stricken land and they have helped. And now working for Gift of the Givers they may take heart in the opportunity to become breadwinners for their families. Macfarlane Moleli: And what is it like interacting with the farmers or the people you go and help? Riaan Mathews: For me it is something nice because you are helping people that needs the stuff so for me it is almost like a blessing I am receiving. And in there faces you can see they are really happy when you come there by them. Macfarlane Moleli: What is it like leaving Hanover and then going to meet the farmers and interacting? Keanu Baartman: It is a wonderful experience. We see stuff we never see. The animals and so. It is great man because we are just almost in a corner here in Hanover park so it is great exploring. Riaan Mathews: There wasn't an income for me. I got married so now I can help my wife; I can help my baby with whatever he wants. Mac hugs. V/O Sadly, one of the volunteers of the Givers, Ameerodien Noordien, was killed in October this year when he was caught in gang crossfire. Macfarlane Moleli: Tell me about the day Ameerodien got shot. Were you with him? Keanu Baartman; Yeh I was with him. In fact it was here opposite by the shop. He just went into the shop to buy something. He didn't get a chance to buy. I just heard a lot of shots so when I look it was him and he was dead on the spot. Ali Sablay: He was caught in a gang crossfire where unfortunately he was deaf in the one ear so when people shouted run, they started to shoot, the time he turned around it was too late. He already had 4 bullets pumped into him and he died immediately on the scene. V/O Prompted by Noordien’s sad fate, the farmers have created a fund to give something back to a community that has touched their lives. AJ Burger: Toe het ons daai tragiese ongeluk gehad van die fodder boys wat die voer vir ons kom aflaai wat toe nou doodgeskiet is in Hanover Park (we had the tragic death of one of the fodder boys who delivered the feed) en ons boere het toe besluit (and we as farmers decided) Dit is eintlik erg om te dink dat mense wat jou help word doodgeskiet en ons het n fonds geskiet vir sy familie om hulle te help. (It is actually bad to think that people who help you are getting killed. We created a fund for the family to help them) So ek wil net se onder elke gebleikte hemp is nog n warm hart vir suid afrika se gemeenskap. (So I just want to say: there is a warm heart beating underneath every worn shirt for the community of South Africa). ___________________________________________________________________________ Sunday Promo: They are known as the volunteers from Hanover in the Cape Flats delivering with them feed to farm animals but with it hope for the Karoo farmers who are struggling with the drought. Promos: 10 seconds V/O Rescued from the Cape Flats where gangs rule the streets, a group of young men has become a symbol of hope for Karoo farmers delivering feed for their starving sheep. 15 seconds V/O The Karoo is experiencing the worst drought in a century, but a group of young men from the terrorised streets of Hanover Park has been sent to deliver feed for their starving animals. Abraham van Wyk: My oupa het voor hy dood is al gese: “My boeta, twee goeters waarvan jy seker is in ons wereld, is dood en droogte.” (Before my grandfather died he said “My son, there are two things in this world you can be certain of, death and drought) 15 seconds V/O Hope came in the form of a group of young men from one of the country’s toughest hoods delivering animal feed to the farmers in the Karoo. Dr Gideon Groenewald: As ons die boere nie help nie, gaan ons 104 duisend ooie moet slag voordat hulle van die dors doodgaan. (If we don’t help the farmers we will have to slaughter 104 000 ewes before they die of thirst). 30 seconds V/O They are known as the Volunteers of the Givers, a group of young men from the gang-ridden streets of Hanover Park, delivering animal feed to the Karoo farmers facing the worst drought in a century. AJ Burger: Hy kom: “‘Hello, Oom, hoe gaan dit met jou? Ons het vir jou voer gebring.” (He says: “Hello uncle, how are you? We’ve brought feed for you.”) En die droogte het daarin n rol gespeel om verskillende mense ook bymekaar te bring. (And the drought has played a role in this to bring different people together.) Hulle bring hoop; hulle bring n lekker atmosfeer wanneer die voer afgelaai word. Dis lekker om met die manne te werk. (They bring hope and a lovely atmosphere when the feed is offloaded. It is nice to work with them.) Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for The Fodder Boys (5330) Annalise Lubbe 16 November 2018

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): They are called the ‘fodder boys.’ A group of youngsters from the Cape flats giving hope to farmers who are facing the worst drought in 200 years and are unable to feed their animals.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Farmers are on their knees praying for rain. Drought has taken its toll in large parts of the country. Sutherland has seen the worst: farmers have sold their prize animals for as little as R30 to avoid starvation. Hope came in the form of the fodder boys: A group of young men rescued from Hannover on the Cape Flats by an NGO who are now delivering feed to desperate farmers in drought crisis. In Sutherland alone sheep stock have dropped from 400 000 to 104 000. Some farmers have sold up their last belongings and moved to start a new life, but for most of them there is no alternative. Farming is in their blood and survive they will. The fodder boys have changed their lives and made it bearable as they receive feed to keep their animals alive until the rain comes back again.
metadata.Summary: Imtiaz Sooliman is the founder Gift of the Givers, a nonprofit organisation that move into areas where disaster has struck and people have lost everything. Instead of despair, they bring relief. From victims of fire to areas where drought has claimed its toll, they work tirelessly to help those in need. In January this year Sooliman looked at the youngsters in Hannover who live in fear of gangsters and drug lords and tasked Ali Sablay from the organization to select a group of youngsters from Hanover Park to join the organisation as volunteers. The Western Cape has been called the murder capital of South Africa. Ten of the 30 police stations with the highest incidence of murder are found in this province and 808 gang related murders alone last year. For the community of Hannover there is little hope of leading a peaceful life and the prospect of work. It is against this landscape that Sablay took the 10 youngsters under his wing. None of them had any prospect of work but already the burden of responsibility were weighing heavily on their shoulders; parents and younger siblings were looking at them to put bread on the table. Set against this backdrop the fodder boys were formed and started working for Gift of the Givers.
metadata.Further information: Since January this year the fodder boys have made a difference to many people’s lives: from delivering blankets and food to victims of fire who have nothing left, to seeing the hope of farmers when they deliver feed for their cattle and sheep, the goodwill they spread in turn has given them hope that life is worth fighting for. He has been counselled to get over the trauma of his best friend’s senseless death.
